default.p.31.outline.0.label: Opening: being glad to sit next to a middle-aged man
default.p.31.outline.0.note: The author points out the paradox of disliking middle-aged men but being happy to sit next to one, while revealing that they once hoped to sit next to a woman.
default.p.31.outline.1.label: The wish to sit next to a woman does not come true
default.p.31.outline.1.note: Explains why the author wants to sit beside a woman—to avoid working—but in reality desire ① almost never comes true.
default.p.31.outline.2.label: The problem of noisy children
default.p.31.outline.2.note: Lists the problems caused by children: making noise, disturbing passengers, preventing others from working, and making it impossible to sleep.
default.p.31.outline.3.label: Moving to the smoking car but still encountering noise
default.p.31.outline.3.note: The author decides to change cars, 「②」, expecting fewer children, but encounters a group of students noisier than children; the expectation is overturned.
default.p.31.outline.4.label: Meeting an elderly person who keeps coughing
default.p.31.outline.4.note: The author expects the elderly person to be quiet, but the person coughs throughout the journey, making the author anxious and unable to work.
default.p.31.outline.5.label: Conclusion: middle-aged men are the most welcome choice.
default.p.31.outline.5.note: After giving up the sweet hope and considering even the possibility of encountering a gang, the author concludes that ③sitting next to a middle-aged man was something to welcome, and in reality ④slept soundly for four hours.

default.p.47.outline.0.label: Paradox: shoji are easy to tear, but that is ①
default.p.47.outline.0.note: Opening with a paradox: shoji screens tear very easily, yet no one demands that they be made stronger—leading into point ①.
default.p.47.outline.1.label: Durable objects make users careless; weak shoji screens cultivate carefulness (A)
default.p.47.outline.1.note: The opposing argument is that sturdy objects make users careless, creating a 'reverse effect'; weak shoji screens force users to be careful and are therefore a form of training. This is the answer to Question 1.
default.p.47.outline.2.label: A new perspective: how to repair modern technological devices (B)
default.p.47.outline.2.note: The author shifts to the perspective of repairs, contrasting it with the modern practice of replacing an entire unit and discarding usable parts, in preparation for the contrast with shoji.
default.p.47.outline.3.label: Repairing the shoji makes them more beautiful than before — ② (C)
default.p.47.outline.3.note: Concludes point ②: after repair, the shoji became more beautiful than before by adding maple-leaf-patterned colored paper, demonstrated by the figures 100→130 and the story of a Paris designer. Supports the answer to Question 2 and the sentence insertion position in Question 3, between C and D.
default.p.47.outline.4.label: Conclusion: repairs nurture affection between people and objects (D)
default.p.47.outline.4.note: The concluding point of the entire passage: repairing things is the source of affection for objects and connects people with machines. This is the main answer to Question 4 about the author's message.
